---
title: "3 Homework: decisions, price and watch, with an agent"
---

Three exercises for after Session 3. In each you direct an AI coding agent and then check what
it produced against the repository. All three are about the layer between a model and a
decision — a policy value, a measure, a what-if — which is where a correct model most often
produces a wrong answer.

**Before you start.** Work on `main` (`git checkout main`), at the repository's root. Each
answer goes in `wiki/homework/_answers/<ID>.md`, a folder git ignores. Scripts the agent
writes belong in a scratch folder outside the repository, and nothing under `adjudication/`,
`pricing/`, `ews/` or `app/` changes. Each self-check recomputes through the module's own
functions and never trusts a number pasted into your answer:

```bash
python -m wiki.homework.check <ID>
```

Each solution below was written by running the exercise with an agent (Claude Code) in this
repository, including where its first attempt went wrong. Try the exercise before you open
it.

## H3.1 Build: move a policy threshold {#h3-1}

**Kind:** Build. **Prompt card:**
[`workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H3.1.md`](https://github.com/aayancheng/banking-analytics-workshop/blob/main/workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H3.1.md).
**Answer:** `wiki/homework/_answers/H3.1.md`.

**Goal.** The credit committee proposes raising the DSCR knockout floor from
{{< var adj.policy.dscr_floor >}} to {{< var adj.dscr_whatif.floor >}}, the upper edge of the
thin-margin override. Have the agent re-run `decide` over all applicants, as the portal
decides them — a description of what the platform decides, not a performance measure, since
four in five of those rows trained the model — with that one value moved; report the decision mix before and after and how
many decisions change; and explain the shift from `adjudication/src/policy.py`. The policy
file stays as committed. The layer itself is described in
[D5.3](../mdd/adjudication/methodology.qmd#adj-policy-layer); D5.6 moves the PD cutoffs the
same way ([cutoff sensitivity](../mdd/adjudication/sensitivity.qmd#cutoff-sensitivity)).

**Check:** `python -m wiki.homework.check H3.1` — it re-runs `decide` both ways, and wants the
number of changed decisions, the new count or share of each decision, the population they are
counted on, a statement in words that Approve does not change and the rule that explains it,
no Approve count or share other than the committed one, and nothing changed under
`adjudication/`.

**The trap.** The expected answer. Raise a knockout floor and you expect fewer approvals; an
agent that writes its explanation before it reads the counts will explain a fall that did
not happen. The other trap is the tool: editing `policy_config.json` is not a what-if, it is a
change to the platform that every later module reads.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**The prompt that worked** is the card as written. What made it work is step 3: the script
printed a cross-tab of old against new decisions, not only the totals.

**The agent's reply** (excerpt):

> | Decision | Committed | `dscr_floor` raised |
> |---|---|---|
> | Approve | {{< var adj.book.Approve.n >}} | {{< var adj.dscr_whatif.Approve.n >}} |
> | Refer | {{< var adj.book.Refer.n >}} | {{< var adj.dscr_whatif.Refer.n >}} |
> | Decline | {{< var adj.book.Decline.n >}} | {{< var adj.dscr_whatif.Decline.n >}} |
>
> Over all {{< var adj.n_applicants >}} applicants, as the portal decides them,
> {{< var adj.dscr_whatif.flipped >}} decisions change, and every one moves from Refer to
> Decline. No Approve changes. An applicant whose DSCR lies between the old floor and the new
> one could never be approved: if its PD put it in the Approve zone, the thin-affordability
> override (`dscr < dscr_refer_hi`) already sent it to Refer. Raising the knockout floor to
> the override's upper edge turns the files the override was holding into Declines — and
> leaves the override with nothing to catch.

**Where it first went wrong.** It did not, and the reason is worth copying: the cross-tab was
in the script before any explanation was written, and the count of committed Approves with a
DSCR below the new floor — {{< var adj.dscr_whatif.approve_below_floor >}} — settled the
Approve row by measurement rather than by argument. The last sentence of the reply is a
finding in its own right: after the change, one of the policy's rules can never fire, the
same kind of dead rule D5 raises as finding 2
([5.7](../mdd/adjudication/limitations.qmd#adj-finding-2)).

**Rehearsed.** An answer that gives the committed Decline count as the new one fails ("the
new Decline count or share is missing"); so does one that gives Approve a new count, one that
never says Approve is unchanged, one whose explanation names no rule for the Approve row, and
any answer while `policy_config.json` is modified.
:::

## H3.2 Catch: "mispricing is worst in band D" {#h3-2}

**Kind:** Catch. **Prompt card:**
[`workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H3.2.md`](https://github.com/aayancheng/banking-analytics-workshop/blob/main/workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H3.2.md)
— it carries the transcript to catch. **Answer:** `wiki/homework/_answers/H3.2.md`.

**Goal.** An agent tells the pricing desk that mispricing is worst in band D. Find the word
that hides a choice, have both readings measured with `price_population` and
`portfolio_summary`, and write an answer in which every "worst" says by what measure. D6 reads
the same table in [6.5](../mdd/pricing/performance.qmd#pr-by-band).

**Check:** `python -m wiki.homework.check H3.2` — it prices the book, then wants the band with
the highest mispriced share named beside its share, and a sentence of your own — not only a
table or a list — saying that band is worst by share; the band with the most mispriced EAD
named beside its amount (in millions, in billions or as the full figure); and no sentence
that calls that band worst by share, "by every measure", or without a money measure. The
transcript's claim, quoted, does not count against you; "band D has the highest PD" is not a
claim about mispricing.

**The trap.** The story fits the wrong answer. "The riskiest band has the most mispricing"
sounds like risk management, and by money it is true. By share of loans it is not — and the
share is what tells a pricing desk where its quotes are most often wrong. Session 3's
recording carries a correction card at exactly this point.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**The prompt that worked** is the card as written.

**The agent's reply** (excerpt):

> | Band | Mispriced share | Mispriced EAD |
> |---|---|---|
> | AAA | {{< var pricing.band.AAA.mispriced_rate >}} | \${{< var pricing.band.AAA.mispriced_ead >}} |
> | A | {{< var pricing.band.A.mispriced_rate >}} | \${{< var pricing.band.A.mispriced_ead >}} |
> | B | {{< var pricing.band.B.mispriced_rate >}} | \${{< var pricing.band.B.mispriced_ead >}} |
> | C | {{< var pricing.band.C.mispriced_rate >}} | \${{< var pricing.band.C.mispriced_ead >}} |
> | D | {{< var pricing.band.D.mispriced_rate >}} | \${{< var pricing.band.D.mispriced_ead >}} |
>
> By share of loans, mispricing is worst in the prime bands: {{< var pricing.worst_band >}} at
> {{< var pricing.worst_band_rate >}}, then {{< var pricing.second_band >}} at
> {{< var pricing.second_band_rate >}}. Band D's share is below the book's. By money, band
> {{< var pricing.worst_ead_band >}} is worst: it holds the most mispriced EAD of any band, because it is the largest band. The
> claim is half right.

**Where it first went wrong.** In the checking, twice. The first run of the check failed the
answer on its own title, which quoted the claim being caught; the check now ignores a claim
inside quotation marks, a heading or a blockquote. A review then showed the opposite fault:
the check passed the transcript's own conclusion — "mispricing is worst in band D", with its
dollar figure — as long as a table elsewhere listed the shares. A table is not a claim. The
check now wants the share reading said in a sentence.

What the agent did not say, and a reviewer should: the level of mispricing is a property of
the generated quotes, which carry no capital charge
([D6.7, finding 1](../mdd/pricing/limitations.qmd)). The *pattern* across bands is measured;
why the best bands miss most often is explained in 6.5 only as a reading of the generator's
code. An answer that turns the table into advice for a real pricing desk has gone further
than the data allows.
:::

## H3.3 Audit: a what-if that re-tiers from a rounded column {#h3-3}

**Kind:** Audit. **Prompt card:**
[`workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H3.3.md`](https://github.com/aayancheng/banking-analytics-workshop/blob/main/workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H3.3.md)
— it carries the code to audit. **Answer:** `wiki/homework/_answers/H3.3.md`.

**Goal.** The card gives a short what-if function for the early-warning tiers. With no
arguments it returns the batch tiers, so its simplest test passes. Have the agent test it the
way a screen with sliders calls it — with the committed cutoffs sent explicitly — and report
every account it gets wrong, the cause, whether its docstring is true, and the fix. The
requirement is the one the workbench is held to: a what-if with the committed values equals
the batch, exactly ([D7.9](../mdd/ews/gate.qmd)).

**Check:** `python -m wiki.homework.check H3.3` — it re-runs the defect from
`score_population`'s own columns, and wants every account it re-tiers named by ID, the cause
(what was done to the stored `prob`), the fix (which probability to re-tier from), and nothing
changed under `ews/` or `app/`. It does not judge the test you propose; read that yourself.

**The trap.** The easy test passes, and the failure is small: a handful of accounts out of
{{< var ews.n_book >}}. "Immaterial" is the wrong verdict. A what-if that moves a loan to
another tier when nothing was changed is lying, and a reviewer who sees it once stops trusting
every screen.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**The prompt that worked** is the card as written.

**The agent's finding** (excerpt):

> With no cutoffs the what-if returns the batch tiers. With the committed cutoffs sent
> explicitly it re-tiers {{< var ews.rounded_retier.n_flipped >}} accounts:
>
> | Account | Batch | What-if | `prob` unrounded | cutoff |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | {{< var ews.rounded_retier.flip1.business_id >}} | {{< var ews.rounded_retier.flip1.batch >}} | {{< var ews.rounded_retier.flip1.rounded >}} | {{< var ews.rounded_retier.flip1.prob >}} | {{< var ews.rounded_retier.flip1.cutoff >}} |
> | {{< var ews.rounded_retier.flip2.business_id >}} | {{< var ews.rounded_retier.flip2.batch >}} | {{< var ews.rounded_retier.flip2.rounded >}} | {{< var ews.rounded_retier.flip2.prob >}} | {{< var ews.rounded_retier.flip2.cutoff >}} |
>
> The book moves from High {{< var ews.tier.High.n >}}, Medium {{< var ews.tier.Medium.n >}},
> Low {{< var ews.tier.Low.n >}} to High {{< var ews.rounded_retier.book.High.n >}}, Medium
> {{< var ews.rounded_retier.book.Medium.n >}}, Low {{< var ews.rounded_retier.book.Low.n >}}.
>
> **Cause.** `score_population` decides `risk_tier` on the unrounded probability but stores
> `prob` rounded to {{< var ews.rounded_retier.dp >}} decimal places. Both accounts sit just
> below a cutoff; rounding puts them exactly on it, and `risk_tier` compares with `>=`, so
> they move up a tier.
>
> **The docstring is false.** The stored column is not "the best probability available": the
> model is committed, and `predict_proba` on `compute_ews_features` — what `score_population`
> runs before rounding — gives the unrounded value.
>
> **Fix.** Re-tier from the unrounded probability on every path, and drop the no-cutoffs
> shortcut so there is one path for every call. Test it by sending the committed cutoffs
> explicitly and requiring every tier in the book to equal the batch.

**Where it first went wrong.** Not in the audit: the card prescribes the explicit-cutoff call,
and the defect showed on the first run. It went wrong in this repository's history. The workbench's
first build had this defect: the agent that built it wrote the defect and the false docstring
beside it, with a test that sent an empty body — which took the shortcut and passed. The
final review caught it before the workbench was merged, by sending what the browser actually
sends. The fix is `retier_book` in
`app/v2/ews_whatif.py`, and `tests/test_app_v2_ui_bodies.py` now pins every tier in the book
under the bodies the screen sends. A test of the path nobody calls proves nothing about the
path everybody does.
:::

## Check your own work

After any exercise, `python verify.py` should still pass. If it does not, the agent changed
something it was told not to: `git status` shows what, and `git checkout -- <path>` puts it
back.
